en: The Supplement on the Characteristics of Svarabhakti:
Now, therefore, I shall fully expound the Śikṣā characterized by all its defining features in brief; therein, eight vowels are proclaimed. (1)
The *tairovirāma*, the *kṣaipra*, the *tairovyañjaka*, the *bhāvya*, the *abhinihita*, the *jātya*, and the *pādavṛtta* as the seventh—
these are to be known as the *praśliṣṭa* [sandhis]; now their characteristics are being declared.
If there is an *udātta* accent on an *avagraha*, that which follows it shall be *svarita*.
One should know that the syllable following the *avagraha* possesses the first accent (*udātta*). Its application should be understood from the example "gopatau," as in "go | patau."

When the vowels *i* and *u* are in the place of [the *praśleṣa* vowels] *ī* and *ū*, and both are acute (*udātta*), they become *y* and *v* respectively within a word that is otherwise always unaccented (*anudātta*); this is proclaimed as the "quick" (*kṣipra*) sandhi. Examples such as *tryambakaṃ* and *dvānnam* should be understood by the discerning.
Whatever word is seen in the Vedic corpus (chandas) with a svarita accent,
if it is preceded by an udātta, that entire word is called *tairovyañjana*.
This is observed in cases such as *iḍe*, *rante*, *havye*, and *kāmye*.

When the vowel *a* is carried away by a single acute *r*, that is called *abhinihita*; "you are a cock" (*kukkuṭo 'si*) is the illustration. Where a vowel is seen with a circumflex (*svarita*) accent within a word due to its opening [of the mouth], [that is the *kṣaipra*].

That accent is a *pādavṛtta*; "putra īdhe" is the illustration. Where the vowel *i* is udātta and joined with the particle *ekāra*, that is to be known as *praśliṣṭa*; "abhīmam" and so forth are the illustrations. 9–10.

When a word beginning with *s* follows a preceding word ending in *k*, it should be understood as having the same sound (*kasavarṇa*), according to the vision of Bhiṣaksīsa. Likewise, when a word beginning with *t* follows a preceding word ending in *c*. (11)
There would be no counter-objection regarding that which is the perception "I am.
When there is a subsequent word beginning with *s* and a preceding word ending in *ṅ*, the perception there is "prāṅksoma," involving two *ka*-colored [consonants]. 12–13.
One should understand that when a word beginning with *sa* follows and a word ending in *na* precedes, they form a *tasa-varṇa*; this is illustrated by three examples.
When a word beginning with *ma* follows and a word ending in *mā* is pronounced before it...
In that case, there should be the same color; this is the view [of the masters].
(15) One should recognize the letter *ja* in the middle of a word or at the beginning or end of a word when it is joined with *ṛ*, *r*, or *y*, as in the example "yuñjāna" and so forth. (16)
It is taught that in Vedic usage, the letter *ṣ* may be pronounced as *kh* between the *ṭ*-class consonants;

the counter-example for this is cited as "pṛṣṭo divīṣe tvā. Furthermore, when a sibilant (*ūṣman*) follows a *repha*, it is pronounced with an *i*-vowel (*saikāra*), provided it is not followed by a consonant (*hal*).
"Of the ancestors here, of the ancestors there," and so forth, is an illustration. The syllable *aṃ* occurs in place of the anusvāra when followed by *ś*, *l*, or *r*.
A short vowel becomes long, and a long vowel becomes short, [in such cases]; furthermore, this is considered a "heavy" (*guru*) syllable. 19.
In the conjunction [of the letters], there is the illustration beginning with "haṃsa," and likewise the [passages] beginning with "tāṃ savituḥ" and "damṣṭrā.
Here, the short, long, and heavy pronunciations must be performed according to their respective order.
In the absence of *śa* and *ra*, *siṃhī* is cited as a counter-example (21). When followed by *śa* or *ra*, the second vowel among those containing *ra* becomes doubled;
likewise, when following a *visarga*, the example is that which is devoid of *ṛ*. (22)
"Unspilled today [be] for someone; Kṛṣṇa is yours"—thus in sequence;
"Sūrya is your father, O Ādya"—and then "May he sustain us"—thus in sequence;
"The great ones on the sacrificial grass"—this is again the illustration for the *kratu*.
The doubling [of a consonant] everywhere is proclaimed by two sūtras of Pāṇini (6.1.1 and 6.1.2).
However, when *y* or *v* follow, there shall be no doubling of *s* in the Vedic language (*chandas*), as in the example:
"May the Vasus fumigate you; its womb according to its proper order. (RV 10.17.12) 24–25.

The letter *ṛ* is prescribed as *hal*, while the letter *re* is traditionally taught in the Vedic language (*chandas*). Examples include *pitṝṇām* for *pitṝṇām*, and so forth. In its own domain, within the context of *saṃhitā*, a short vowel may sometimes become long.
The vowels (varṇa) are joined with *hal* and *visarga*, and they are not joined with *hal* or *yuta*. [In the rule] "sapaktnānyaddhvamagghnyā," there may be some lengthening here;
however, in cases such as "bhāgam prajāvatī," there is shortness and not length. 27–28.
"Due to the combination of *hal* (consonants) and *ut* (vowels), this should be understood by the wise"—thus is the manner of pronouncing phonemes described in the *Kātyāyana-Parīśiṣṭa*.
"The euphonic combinations (*sandhi*) are to be known as fourfold, arising from elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), and modification (*vikāra*). (29)
And likewise, in that context, there is first the illustration by way of the base (*prakṛti*), and then by way of the modification (*vikāra*), as in "preṣitā" and so forth;
and in [the mantra] beginning with "devo vaḥ savitā," there is the demonstration of the base and so on. (30)
When both vowels are present and no *sandhi* (euphonic junction) is perceived between them, that is known by the wise as *vivṛtti*; one should perceive it as being exactly that.
This is to be understood as fourfold; the first is the *pipīlikā*.

The four transformations are: the matured (pākavatī), the following the calf (vatsānusāriṇī), and the one whose calf has been released (vatsānutsṛjitā). An ant, long at its beginning and end but thin in the middle, serves as an illustration.
The second [verse], however, has both short vowels; "vina indra" is the illustration.
The third is declared to have long vowels; "tāsyā" is the illustration.
At the end, the fourth would have long vowels; "tānāvoḍham aśvinā" is the illustration. 34–35.
Svarabhakti is of five kinds; among them, the first is known as kariṇī.
Where a conjunction of the letter *la* with the letter *ha* is observed—as in the example "barhir asi"—that is to be understood as kariṇī. (36)
Where a conjunction of the letter *la* with the letter *ha* is seen, she is to be known as Kurviṇī; thus one perceives her as Upavalhā.
Where a conjunction of the letter *ra* with the letter *śa* is seen, [she is to be known as Śaurpiṇī]. 37–38.
That [meter] is to be known as Hariṇī, according to the view beginning with "of one having hemorrhoids" (arśasaḥ) and so forth;
where a conjunction arises between the letter *la* and the letter *śa*, one should recognize that as Hariṇī, according to the view of Śatavalśā. 39.
Furthermore, where a conjunction of the letter *ra* with the letter *ṣa* is observed—
as in *haṃsapāda*, *vijñeyā*, *varṣo*, and *varṣīyasī*—
this has been declared as the characteristic of *svarabhakti* by the learned. 40–41.
"Having known this, a man goes to the eternal world of Brahman"—
thus was this supplementary treatise (pariśiṣṭa) composed with joy by Kātyāyana himself.
(42) Thus ends the Śikṣā on the characteristics of vowel-attachment (svarabhakti) as spoken by Kātyāyana.
